title: KB Toys (1922–2009): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: KB Toys from a Pittsfield candy wholesaler to 1,322 stores, a leveraged buyout, two bankruptcies and a name that is still for sale, read through its owner’s SEC filings and a Delaware court opinion.

card.blurb: The toy store in the mall. It had 1,322 stores when Walmart started selling the season’s hottest toys below cost, and a buyout that had already taken about $120 million out.

hero.dates: Founded Apr 1, 1922. Filed for its second Chapter 11 on Dec 11, 2008 and closed its stores in early 2009.
hero.standfirst: For three decades it was the toy store you walked past on the way to somewhere else. Then the shoppers stopped walking past.
hero.deck: KB Toys began as a candy wholesaler in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, and became the largest mall-based toy chain in the United States. It was sold three times in twenty years, the last time in a leveraged buyout that paid its owners about $120 million before a price war with Walmart and Target sent it into bankruptcy. The record is the SEC filings of the company that owned it, a Delaware court opinion, contemporary press and the archived website.

findings.title: Its public owner took a large loss to be rid of it.
findings.text: Consolidated Stores bought Kay-Bee in 1996 for about $315M and sold it in 2000 for gross proceeds of about $305M, recording a $430.8M after-tax loss on disposal of the toy segment.[^1][^5]

findings.title: The buyout was almost all borrowed money.
findings.text: Forbes reported that Bain put down $18.1M in cash and that KB borrowed about $237M. Sixteen months later KB borrowed again to fund an $85M payment to Bain.[^17]

findings.title: No court ruled that the dividend killed it.
findings.text: A Delaware judge dismissed the seller’s lawsuit in 2006, and the creditors’ case was settled on terms that were not disclosed.[^7][^25][^28]

findings.title: The price war did the visible damage.
findings.text: Sales at stores open at least a year fell 10% in 2003 while discounters cut average toy prices by 8%, and KB skipped vendor payments that December.[^18]

findings.title: It failed again without the buyout debt.
findings.text: Under a new owner and with fewer than half the stores, comparable sales fell 20% between October 5 and December 8, 2008, and the chain chose to liquidate.[^23]
